summary: Describes the Common Indexing Protocol framework: its architecture and how servers exchange indices of the information they hold, so searches can be directed to the right place.

eli5.summary: Libraries trade lists of what books they have, so you can be pointed to the right one without visiting each.

questions: what is the common indexing protocol
how does cip index passing work
subtitle: How servers swap compact summaries of their data so searches can be sent to the right place.

tldr.problem: In a distributed database system, a server knows only its own data, so a search must either be copied to every server or the client has to guess where to look.
tldr.mechanism: CIP lets servers pass index objects (a header plus an opaque payload summarizing a dataset) to peer servers. A server uses the indices it holds to send clients referrals toward the datasets that may have the answer.
tldr.outcome: CIP is a Proposed Standard framework. It defines how indices move and combine, while the index formats themselves and the transports live in companion documents.

today: RFC 2651 is a Proposed Standard published in August 1999, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is one of three CIP documents, alongside RFC 2652 and RFC 2653.

sections.title: Why CIP Exists
sections.content:
The Common Indexing Protocol (CIP) passes indexing information from server to server to make query routing possible. Query routing means redirecting and replicating queries through a distributed database system toward the servers that hold the desired results.

CIP grew out of the indexing part of the Whois++ Directory Service (RFC 1913, RFC 1914). There the index object, the centroid, was tied to template-based databases and token matching. CIP pulls indexing out of the data access protocol and makes the index object abstract so it fits other kinds of information retrieval. It also replaces Whois++'s ad-hoc data representations with structures based on MIME.

This document specifies CIP version 3, described as a major overhaul. Through a short negotiation sequence, version 3 servers can interoperate with earlier servers in an index-passing mesh.
sections.eli5: Some systems already traded lists of what they held, but only in one fixed style. CIP makes the list style flexible so many kinds of collections can use it.

sections.title: Indexes and Query Routing
sections.content:
CIP is a "backend" protocol, spoken only among servers. The same servers still speak a normal data access protocol, such as LDAP, Whois++, HTTP or Z39.50, to their clients. Queries and referrals travel over that native protocol. Index objects travel by the means this framework defines.

Without indexing, no server knows about any other. With it, a server can answer from its local dataset and also from indices received from peers. An index is a possibly reduced version of a remote dataset, not a copy, so the reply may be a referral to another dataset rather than a complete answer. Creating, sending and storing indices costs resources, and query routing is what that investment buys.

The client stays in charge. It is always the client's job to collate, filter and chase the referrals it receives, which gives the user or agent the most control over resolution. A proxy could chase referrals on behalf of simple clients.

Because no single index suits every query (a plain keyword list cannot say whether two keywords were near each other), index objects are abstract. Each type must be defined by a separate specification, and this document covers only how indices move among servers.
sections.eli5: Your library keeps its own books and also a few lists from other libraries. If it cannot help, it tells you which library to try, and you do the walking yourself.

sections.title: The Index Object
sections.content:
A CIP index object has two parts: a header and a payload. The header holds the metadata needed to process the index. The payload holds the index itself and is opaque to CIP; only the specification for that object type says how to parse and use it.

Three headers matter most:

  • type selects which index object specification governs how the index is created, parsed and used.
  • DSI, the Dataset Identifier, uniquely identifies the dataset the index was built from.
  • Base-URI holds one or more URIs that form the basis of any referral generated from the index. It also constrains which kinds of aggregation are possible when a mesh speaks several protocols.

The exact header syntax is given in the companion MIME document, RFC 2652.
sections.eli5: An index object is a package with a label on the outside (what kind, which collection, where to go) and a sealed list inside that only the matching rulebook can read.

sections.title: Meshes and Index Passing
sections.content:
A CIP mesh is a set of servers that pass indices of the same type among themselves. It is typically a hierarchical tree, with servers nearer the root holding larger, more comprehensive indices. Lateral links are explicitly allowed, there can be more than one root-like part, and administrators are encouraged, but not obliged, to avoid loops. Mixing index types in one mesh is undefined and called dangerous. A server that receives an unknown index type can pass it on untouched, or it should return an appropriate error.

Two servers cooperate in one of two relationships:

  • Polling. The polled server holds the data and generates the index. The polling server collects it. The polled server notifies the poller of new indices, and the poller may fetch at once or schedule it, and may also ask for a new index at any time.
  • Index pushing. A server simply sends its index to a peer whenever necessary, and the receiver may refuse it, accept it, discard it, filter it or take it as is. This suits simple leaf nodes that do not implement the full CIP transaction protocol.

Index passing runs over reliable transports, including TCP connections and Internet mail messages, as described in the transport document (RFC 2653). The text suggests it should run as a parallel, possibly lower-priority job beside answering queries.
sections.eli5: Libraries can swap lists in two ways. In one, they ask each other and say when their list changed. In the other, a small library just mails its list to anyone and lets them do what they want with it.

sections.title: Combining Indices (Aggregation)
sections.content:
A server may pass any index in its local index (built from its own data) or its in-bound indices (collected from others) through unchanged. It may also aggregate two or more into a single new out-bound index, which cuts redundancy at the cost of longer referral chains.

Aggregation is allowed if and only if all three conditions hold:

  • Every index covers exactly the same set of protocols, judged by the scheme of each Base-URI.
  • The server supports every one of those data access protocols.
  • The specification for the index type explicitly defines the aggregation operation.

The result must carry Base-URIs characteristic of the local server for each protocol it supports, and should carry the local server's DSI. The first condition guards against sending a client down a referral chain through servers that do not speak the protocol it used, which would cut off any hits beyond that point.

Aggregation trades indexing overhead against referral chain length. The text says this tradeoff still needs exploring in operational use, and managers may disable aggregation for performance reasons.
sections.eli5: A big library can merge several small lists into one shorter list. That saves paper, but you may have to ask more libraries before you find your book.

sections.title: Referrals and Navigating the Mesh
sections.content:
A server makes a referral when a search of its index objects shows that a dataset may hold hits. If several indices point to the same dataset, it should send only one referral, since the client may not detect duplicates. The referral travels in the native protocol, so its syntax is not a CIP matter, but at the least it must carry a DSI and a URI. The DSI lets the client avoid referral loops, and the URI comes from the Base-URI. A DSI-Description header should be included when available, as a friendlier label for the user. For an LDAP server, the Base-URI also carries the X.500 subtree the index was made for.

Each data access protocol needs defined rules to map its queries onto searches of an index type. For LDAP with the centroid type, attribute names must be mapped and queries tokenized under the centroid indexing policy. These rules belong in the index object specification.

Clients can show raw referrals to the user, ask which to follow, or follow all automatically within time and bandwidth limits. Because the mesh may contain cycles, a client that follows everything needs a mesh traversal algorithm; the one documented for Whois++ in RFC 1914 works unchanged if its handle is read as a DSI. Clients should start from a well-connected local server rather than a single root, and can widen the search by asking which server polls it.
sections.eli5: When the library points you elsewhere, it writes down the collection's name and address. The name stops you from visiting the same place twice.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC names three concerns. Indices can leak too much proprietary information unless carefully controlled, so an index type must keep the risk of reverse engineering the database at a level matching the value of the data. The protocol itself needs external security services to operate safely. And CIP can be used to spread false information: a false index can selectively prune parts of a mesh, and CIP provides no method for trusting the data it carries.
sections.eli5: A list of what you own can give away too much, and someone could hand out a fake list. CIP does not check who is telling the truth.
